_README: Research-confirmed facts about places the automated sources can't see.
The GIS layers only know what someone has mapped. A town park with no
OpenStreetMap trail tagged inside it comes out 'unverified' even when a
single web search proves it has trails, parking and a pavilion. This file
is where that human research lands.
Entries are matched on name + town and applied AFTER the automated pass,
so they override it. Every entry must carry `source` and `checked` — a
claim without a citation is a guess, and guesses are what this file
exists to replace.
Fields you can set: trails, parking, water, waterName, waterType, sports,
sportList, playground, historic, beach, pool, dogpark, fee, url, note,
agency, acres.
`rules` entries match on type/subtype/agency instead of a single name, so one cited regulation can settle hundreds of places at once. Same requirement: source and checked date.
THIS FILE IS NEVER REGENERATED. places.json is rebuilt from scratch every
month and anything typed into it is destroyed; this file is the only place
in the pipeline meant to be edited by hand, and the workflow's commit step
names its files explicitly so it can never touch this one.
Add `at: [lat, lng]` to any match block. Names change upstream — a source
re-spells a park and the entry silently stops applying — but locations
don't. If the name lookup fails, the nearest place within 600 m wins, so
the research survives the rename.
Every run writes data/research-audit.json, and the workflow fails if any
entry or rule matched nothing. That failure is deliberate: research going
quietly missing is invisible in the output, because the output still looks
perfectly fine without it.

places.note: Roughly 100 acres of town open space at 158 Town Farm Road. Hiking and unmarked trails, a pond, and a reservable pavilion with picnic tables and grills. Leashed dogs welcome.

places.rename: Lucius Pond Ordway – Devil's Den Preserve
places.note: 1,746 acres across Weston and Redding — the largest preserve in Fairfield County, with a 20-mile trail system. Open dawn to dusk. Main parking at the end of Pent Road, Weston; small pull-off on Dayton Road, Redding.
Part of the Devil's Den preserve complex. Open dawn to dusk; trail maps at the Pent Road parking area in Weston.

places.agency: Yale School Forests (Yale School of the Environment)
places.note: A 7,600-acre working research and teaching forest owned by Yale. The public can hike free of charge on designated routes — notably the blue-blazed Nipmuck Trail loop from Boston Hollow Road and Yale's interpretive trails. The rest of the forest hosts active research and timber operations, so stay on marked trails.

A private nonprofit working forest open to the public daily from sunrise to sunset, free of charge, with over 13 miles of trails for hiking, skiing, snowshoeing and biking. Parking at the East gate off Windrow Road in Norfolk and the West gate in Falls Village; sign in at the gate kiosks. No swimming in ponds or streams.

match.name: City of New London Public Watershed Lands

places.agency: City of New London Water Department
places.note: Drinking-water supply watershed lands around Lake Konomoc and associated reservoirs. The city publishes no public-access or recreation policy for these lands; assume entry is not permitted without checking with the New London Department of Public Utilities.

A 400-acre Nature Conservancy preserve managed by the Salem Land Trust, open to the public with about 6 miles of trails through meadows, woods and wetlands near the East Branch of the Eightmile River. Parking at 119 Hagen Road; catch-and-release fishing allowed, dogs must be leashed. Part of TNC's larger Eightmile River conservation area.

places.fee: Free day use; camping fees apply
places.note: Army Corps of Engineers flood-control land along the Quinebaug River with a 200-acre lake, over 9 miles of marked hiking trails, a boat ramp, canoe launch, free disc golf course, picnicking and a seasonal campground. Day use is free.

places.agency: Eversource / CT DEEP (Cooperative Wildlife Management Area)
places.note: A large forested tract on the west bank of the Connecticut River with about 2.5 miles of blue-blazed trails (Mattabesett and Scovill Loop), Hubbard Brook and a small river beach. Open for hiking, birding and fishing at no charge; trailhead parking off River Road. The River Beach Trail crosses an active rail line at a designated crossing only.

A state Wildlife Management Area protecting Connecticut's largest freshwater wetland, along the Hollenbeck River near Falls Village. Parking off Route 126; open for hunting, wildlife observation and passive recreation, with no formal trail network — expect wet, unmarked terrain and active hunting in season.

match.name: South Meadows Greenway at Goodwin University

places.note: A roughly 3-mile riverside trail along the Connecticut River, maintained by Goodwin University and designated an official Connecticut Greenway. Free and open for walking, biking and cross-country skiing, with accessible parking at the northern trailhead on South Meadow Lane in East Hartford.

A roughly 30-acre island off Greenwich's Byram shore, part of Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge. Open daily from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset with beach and trail access — but there is no ferry or dock, so visitors must arrive by private boat (kayaks may land on designated beaches). Obey posted habitat closures.

Flood-control project land along the Naugatuck River spanning Thomaston, Harwinton, Litchfield and Plymouth. Open for hiking, fishing, picnicking, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, with designated seasonal trail-bike routes; parking and a picnic area near the dam off Route 222. Portions close when the flood pool is holding water.

A 234-acre Winchester Land Trust sanctuary near Winchester Center, open to the public with marked trails past the Rugg Brook headwaters, a beaver marsh and a small waterfall. Park at the end of Preston Road (room for 3-4 cars) or at Hurlbut Field. Dogs on leash; no hunting.

A 380-acre Nature Conservancy preserve on former farmland in Pomfret's Quiet Corner, open free of charge from dawn to dusk. A roughly two-mile hiking route follows an old farm road; park at the head of Old Kings Highway. Passive recreation only — no pets, bikes, hunting or camping.

Town-owned reservoir property at the end of Old Marlborough Turnpike, bordering Meshomasic State Forest. The town lists the Portland Reservoir Rim Trail as a public facility open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily; a well-used loop trail circles the reservoir.

Town open space maintained by the Orange Conservation Commission for passive recreation. A blue-blazed loop trail starts at the parking lot off Derby-Milford Road at the Turkey Hill Road intersection; visitors are asked to stay on marked trails to protect wetlands and vernal pools.

A 700-acre seasonal flood-control reservoir off Route 8 north of Winsted, open to the public at no charge during daylight hours. Boat launch, trout and bass fishing, and wildlife viewing; foot access is allowed year-round, though areas can close on short notice for flood control.

An Audubon sanctuary open daily sunrise to sunset; the Pond Loop Trail circles Miles Pond, known for wildlife viewing. Buildings are not open to the public, and pets, bicycles, swimming and off-trail travel are prohibited.

A roughly 305-acre town preserve of forest, wetlands and ponds on Burma Road. Blazed loop trails (Weigold, Taylor Pond, Julia's, Ruby) start from the parking area at Moose Meadow and Burma Roads; Taylor Pond and the Fenton River are highlights.

match.name: Silvio O. Conte National Fish and Wildlife Refuge

places.rename: Silvio O. Conte NFWR — Salmon River Division
places.note: Part of the four-state Silvio O. Conte refuge, protecting tidal marsh and floodplain forest where the Salmon River meets the Connecticut River. Open daily dawn to dusk for wildlife observation, photography, hunting and fishing — but facilities are minimal, with no marked trails or lots, and one parcel is reachable only by water.

The Appalachian Trail follows the Housatonic River through Kent, including the St. Johns Ledges climb and the River Walk. The trail is free to walk with no fees or permits; trailhead parking on River Road via CT 341 and Skiff Mountain Road.

A 301-acre mostly forested preserve with wetlands and Cranberry Meadow Brook, acquired by the East Lyme Land Trust in 2022. Trailheads on Holmes Road and Grassy Hill Road were planned at purchase, but current trail and access status could not be verified; hunting is permitted on the property. This is not Nehantic State Forest.

This 731-acre attribution appears to be a mapping error: neither National Audubon nor Connecticut Audubon lists a sanctuary of this size in Redding — the only Audubon holding in the town's open-space plan is the 54-acre Edward Steichen Memorial Preserve. Treat this record with caution until the source data is corrected.

Records suggest this is deed-restricted private forest land (a private club is registered under a similar name in Litchfield), not public open space. No public access policy or managing agency could be found — do not assume walking access.

No public open space by this name could be verified in Winchester. The town's similarly named Mountainside Drive parcel (about 118 acres) was offered for sale for development in 2023 and is far smaller than this record claims. Access unconfirmed — treat with caution.

A Connecticut Audubon sanctuary of about 850 acres spanning the Sherman/Pawling line, with roughly 15 miles of trails open dawn to dusk year-round, free of charge. Parking at 57 Wakeman Hill Road. Dogs, bikes and drones are prohibited; a visitor center hosts programs and exhibits.

places.agency: Town of Sherman Park & Recreation Commission
places.note: Sherman's town athletic complex at 17 Sawmill Road, known locally as Veterans Field, with a public walking track, pickleball courts and playing fields. The town's public walking group meets here; no fee is indicated for the grounds.

The Appalachian Trail enters Connecticut from New York at Hoyt Road in Sherman, climbing Ten Mile Hill above the Ten Mile River watershed. Free to walk, no permits; the Connecticut AMC chapter maintains this section, and the adjacent Herrick Preserve connects for loop hikes.

A 185-acre NCLC preserve (originally Naromi Land Trust) with gentle trails through hardwood forest to the Housatonic Overlook, about 1.25 miles each way past stone walls and vernal pools. Park on the west side of Evans Hill Road near Route 55; trails connect to the Appalachian Trail.

match.name: Mildred Strauss and James Morrissey Family Nature Preserves

places.note: A 142-acre NCLC preserve spanning Gaylordsville and Sherman, with a roughly 1.5-mile round-trip trail between trailheads on Gaylord Road and 64 Edmonds Road. A brook fed by underground marble-bedrock channels supports rare plants including orchids. Park at the Gaylord Road pull-out without blocking the gate.

Sherman's town-owned open space at 43 Route 39 North — also called Volunteer Fields in town records, and 'Town Meadows' in older map data. Roughly 115 acres of meadows with mowed walking paths, an uphill stretch with a view, and four pickleball courts completed in 2024. A favorite local spot for walking dogs (leash ordinance applies); roadside parking off Route 39.

A 120-acre NCLC preserve beside Sherman's town center: a boardwalk through a maple wetland, a rolling loop along Sawmill Brook, and steeper yellow and blue trails up Turner Mountain with seasonal views. Park at the Sherman Town Center lot; the trailhead is near 15 Route 39 North.

About 86 acres of hardwood forest where a green-and-white blazed loop of roughly 2.5 miles crosses the Naromiyocknowhusunkatankshunk Brook on stepping stones and footbridges. Trailhead at 18 Crooked Furrows Lane; parking for about 3 cars.

An 81-acre preserve known for massive glacial erratics and a boulder field, with easterly views after leaf-fall and lively vernal pools in spring. Trailhead and gravel parking at 46 CT-37 East. Adjoins Irene's Woods for a longer combined hike.

An 84-acre preserve whose single blazed loop starts with a steep climb, then rolls through forest past historic stone walls and old-growth trees; popular with trail runners and birdwatchers. Roadside parking with a kiosk at 23 Briggs Hill Road. Can be muddy in spring.

Two boardwalks — a 330-foot wheelchair-accessible northern one and a 400-foot southern one — extend into a calcium-rich freshwater marsh with active beavers. A viewing platform overlooks habitat famous for American and Least Bitterns; a designated Important Bird Area. Parking on Route 39 North near Route 55.

Trails lead from Hubbell Mountain Road past vernal pools to a flat-rock overlook, a split rock outcrop, and on to Route 37, with Eagle Scout-built steps through a small stream gorge. Roadside pull-off parking at 15 Hubbell Mountain Road; adjoins Towner Hill Preserve.

Owned by the Northwest Connecticut Land Conservancy, which distinguishes its “over 300 wildlife sanctuaries” from its “31 nature preserves open to the public with hiking trails.” This parcel is not among the public trail preserves, so treat it as a sanctuary without established visitor access; contact NCLC before visiting.

Part of its acreage lies under Candlewood Lake.

A former Naromi Land Trust parcel off Route 39 North, now owned by NCLC. No marked trails or parking are published for it; NCLC land is customarily open to quiet on-foot visits, but check with the conservancy before making a trip.

places.agency: Great Hollow Nature Preserve & Ecological Research Center
places.note: The 'Wesleyan University' attribution is decades stale: Wesleyan deeded this parcel away in 1999, and since 2015 it has been part of Great Hollow Nature Preserve & Ecological Research Center — 825 acres free and open sunrise to sunset, with several miles of trails crossing into Sherman. Main parking and trailhead at 225 Route 37, New Fairfield.

Owned by the Northwest Connecticut Land Conservancy, which distinguishes its “over 300 wildlife sanctuaries” from its “31 nature preserves open to the public with hiking trails.” This parcel is not among the public trail preserves, so treat it as a sanctuary without established visitor access; contact NCLC before visiting.
A small former Naromi Land Trust parcel now held by NCLC. It is not listed among the conservancy's Sherman hiking preserves, and no trailhead, parking or access information has been published.

An NCLC tract within the footprint of the 185-acre Herrick Preserve, which is open daily sunrise to sunset with a moderate lollipop loop to Amy's Lookout and the Housatonic Overlook. Limited roadside parking on Evans Hill Road near Route 55; trails connect to the Appalachian Trail.

Sherman's town park and beach at the north end of Candlewood Lake, off Route 39 at Sawmill Road, with a swimming beach and boat slips. Beach passes are issued to Sherman residents with proof of address, so the beach operates for residents and their guests. 'Colonial Park' is a legacy gazetteer name for this spot.
A private community beach on Green Pond inside Candlewood Lake Estates, owned by the Candlewood Tax District. District rules require a community beach pass; it is not open to the general public.
A private community beach on Green Pond inside Candlewood Lake Estates, owned by the Candlewood Tax District. District rules require a community beach pass; it is not open to the general public.

NCLC conservation land off Upland Pastures Road (former Osborne family farmland, deeded to Naromi Land Trust). Not on NCLC's formal trail-preserve list, but in regular local use for quiet walking — confirmed first-hand. The adjacent Towner Hill Preserve trailhead connects the area.
source: Field-verified in person by the site maintainer (Sherman resident), 2026-08-03

siteRules: Dogs must be leashed (7 ft max)
No motor vehicles off designated roads
rules.why: Connecticut state parks, forests and wildlife management areas are open to the public daily from 8am to sunset by regulation. Walking is permitted throughout, so state land does not need a mapped trail to be reachable.

siteRules: Open 8am to sunset; closed half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise
rules.why: Conn. Agencies Regs. 26-16-3a governs public use of state wildlife management areas. Hiking is permitted; these are working conservation land rather than developed parks.
Municipal and non-profit burying grounds are walk-in public space during daylight. They are not required to have a mapped trail to be visitable.

siteRules: Some preserves restricted for nesting or fragile habitat — check posted signs
rules.why: Avalonia's 46 preserves, over 5,000 acres across nine southeastern Connecticut towns, are open and free to the public dawn to dusk, with trail maps online and posted on site.

siteRules: Some preserves allow bikes or horses — check the preserve page
rules.why: Over 7,500 acres in northeast Connecticut, with about 18 hikeable properties and 16+ miles of trails open to the public. Note: not every Wyndham holding is trailed, so this asserts reachable rather than claiming a trail on each parcel.

siteRules: Open dawn to dusk, year round
rules.why: Flanders manages over 2,400 acres in Woodbury and neighbouring towns. Trails at its seven major preserves are open to the public at no charge, dawn to dusk, year round.
45 trailed nature preserves across Easton, Weston, Westport, Fairfield, Southport, Norwalk and Bridgeport, all open to walk dawn to dusk.

siteRules: Town open space, open to residents and visitors
rules.why: Glastonbury publishes an inventory and map of its town-owned open spaces, many with walking trails. Municipal open space in Connecticut is public; the town cannot exclude non-residents.

siteRules: Passive recreation: hiking, birding, nature study
A few preserves are closed to protect at-risk species — check before visiting
rules.why: Most TNC Connecticut preserves are open free for low-impact recreation. Deliberately not claiming trails, because TNC states some preserves harbouring at-risk species are closed.

siteRules: Municipal open space, open to residents and non-residents alike
rules.why: Land recorded in PAD-US as city or town owned is municipal open space. Under Leydon v. Greenwich (2001) a Connecticut municipality may not close its parks and open space to non-residents, so this land is public by law.
